title: Access Control, Intrusion and Building Automation on One Platform, Not Three
description:
At the ASIS Québec 2026 Symposium this week, ICT put a question to the show floor that New Zealand clients ask us often: can access control, intrusion detection and building automation run as one platform instead of three?

In many Wellington and Auckland buildings, the honest answer today is no. Access control runs on one system, the alarm panel on another and the building management system on a third. Each has its own user database, its own schedules and often its own service contractor. That separation leaves gaps. Someone removed from access control can still hold a valid alarm code, and an after-hours door event never reaches the lighting or HVAC. When we design access control on a unified platform such as ICT's Protege, one credential record controls doors, arming and building responses, and one audit trail shows who did what and when. For clients, that means fewer contractors to coordinate, faster offboarding when staff leave, and incident reviews that take minutes, not days.

If your site runs three systems that should be talking to each other, send us a message to book an access control review.

title: Deepfake Callers Are the New Tailgaters at Your Front Desk
description:
ASIS International's latest Security Management Highlight episode features Tom Cross, head of threat research at GetReal Security, explaining how AI-enabled audio and video now make fake job applicants and fake authorities convincing enough to get hired or leave with confidential information.

For New Zealand businesses, this is a physical security problem as much as a cyber one. Many Wellington and Auckland sites still approve a contractor, reissue a lost card or allow after-hours entry on the strength of a phone or video call. If the voice or face on that call can be faked, the call is no longer verification. The principle we apply to tailgating applies here too: trust the process, not the person in front of you. In practice, that means calling back on a known number before any credential is issued, pre-registering visitors, and access control rules that keep a newly issued card out of sensitive areas until a second person approves it.

title: AI-Augmented Attacks Put Your Building Security Devices on the Agenda
description:
Johnson Controls has released a white paper on AI-augmented attacks against OT systems. It points to the thousands of zero-day vulnerabilities found this year and argues for a zero-trust overlay to protect building systems.

Our view is that New Zealand building owners should treat this as a security integration issue, not only an IT one. Access control controllers, CCTV recorders, intercoms and building management systems are all OT devices. In many Auckland and Wellington buildings they sit on flat networks, use default credentials and run firmware that hasn't been updated since commissioning. If attackers can find vulnerabilities faster, the long patch cycles common in security hardware become a real exposure. When we design a site or take one over, we separate security devices from the corporate network, remove shared and default accounts, record firmware versions and add patching to the maintenance schedule alongside door and alarm testing. When you choose a provider, ask one simple question: who owns the cyber posture of your physical security system? If the answer is nobody, that is the gap.

Send us a message to book a review of how your security devices sit on your network.

title: Matthew Bowles and the Access Control Rebuild Built for the Next Technician
description:
Last week we shared a before and after from a client's access control upgrade. The after photo is Matthew Bowles' work, and it's worth looking at what a rebuild like that involves.

A system that has grown over years usually comes with undocumented cabling, controllers mounted wherever there was space, and terminations only the original installer understood. Matthew's work starts before a single cable is cut. He traces and labels every run, then plans a layout that keeps every connection accessible. He rebuilds with the next technician and the next service visit in mind. It's slow, careful work, and it's why a fault call six months later takes minutes to diagnose instead of hours. It's also the standard we hold across our Wellington and Auckland teams. Quality is built into every decision from the moment work begins, not added at the end.

Thanks, Matthew, for the care and pride you put into this one. If you're a technician who works this way, send us a message. We want to hear from you.

title: From Tangled Legacy Cabinet to a Serviceable Access Control System
description:
A client asked us to upgrade an access control system that had grown and changed over many years. The brief was to replace the hardware. The real job was to make the system easier to maintain, easier to troubleshoot and more reliable for the long term.

The existing system worked, but each change had been layered on top of the last. That made every service visit slower and every fault harder to trace. We treated the upgrade as a rebuild. We mapped the existing system, planned a clean layout and reinstalled it so every cable has a place and every connection stays accessible. The result is a cabinet any qualified technician can open and understand. Future service visits are shorter, maintenance is less likely to cause an accidental disconnection, and the client's new hardware is protected for its full working life. This is why we see the quality of an install as part of the security of the site, not a cosmetic finish.

title: Is a Certificate of Approval Enough for Higher-Risk Security Work?
description:
NZSA's five-day Advanced Security Officer training programme starts in Epsom, Auckland on 9 November. It's built on a clear premise: higher-risk security work demands skills beyond a Certificate of Approval.

The programme covers legal powers and risk assessment, de-escalation, citizen's arrest and proportionate force, and safe restraint and welfare monitoring. It also covers Police handover and evidence, with scenario-based assessment and ongoing competency maintenance. That raises a question every New Zealand business using guarding should ask: is a CoA alone enough for the people you put into those situations? Our position as an integrator is that technology does not replace trained people. CCTV, access control and intercoms show an officer what is happening and record it. The officer still has to make a lawful, proportionate decision in seconds. If you specify guarding for retail, healthcare or after-hours sites, ask providers what training sits above the CoA and how they keep it current.

Where do you stand? Should advanced training be required for higher-risk roles, or left to each provider? Drop a comment below.
